Canberra Airport is looking to flip the script on Sydney and have big acts like Taylor Swift choosing the capital over the harbour city instead.

Login or signup to continue reading

Its proposed indoor lakeside stadium would have a maximum capacity for concerts of 36,000 - almost twice the size of Sydney's Afterpay Arena, which holds up to 21,000.

Canberra Airport chief executive Stephen Byron announced BESIX Watpac as the builder to work with architects Populous on Thursday.

The plan is to have initial designs and costs submitted to the federal government by Christmas - early in the new year at the latest.

Byron ruled out a "Super Stadium", which would include an oval for cricket and Australian rules, with the focus purely on a rectangular venue - for the rugby codes, soccer and indoor concerts and events.

He also said the focus remained on a capacity of 25,000, with the ability to expand to 30,000, while dismissing concerns about parking.

His airport group has had continuing discussions with both levels of government, and will continue talks with the Catholic Church on Friday about purchasing the archbishop's former residence at Regatta Place.

But Byron dropped a bombshell to The Canberra Times that will have the ACT's Swifties - along with fans of the world's other big acts - frothing at the mouth.

While Sydney might have bigger outdoor venues, an indoor venue of 36,000 would take the weather out of the equation and potentially allow Canberra to become the preferred destination.

"We'll have a bigger indoor venue than Sydney has," Byron told The Canberra Times.

"It takes a while for me to get my head around that myself.

"You sort of think, well, seriously, is Taylor Swift going to come here?

"Well, we've got a better venue than [Sydney].

"Now she might opt for the outdoor venue. There's a bit of risk in that.

"We've got a guaranteed venue, no weather impact, 35,000 people.

"You'll sell out five nights in a row and people will come down the road from Sydney.

"How do you feel about that? That's all right for us."

The proposal continues to move at a breakneck pace that's untethered from government red tape.
